While new CVEs and breaches keep dropping, here’s a quick look at what’s been recorded so far in 2026.

The “2Shell” family has been one of the biggest stories this year.  

PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618 & CVE-2026-109619) was actively exploited, including against Check Point gateways where attackers dropped webshells after gaining access.  

React2Shell, Node2Shell/HTTP2Shell, and others in the same pattern followed unauthenticated RCE in widely used components.

Recent additions to CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities list include:  
- CVE-2026-76466 (Cisco Expressway – hard-coded credentials)  
- CVE-2026-123890 (VMware vCenter – authentication bypass)  
- CVE-2026-129448 (Apache Roller – deserialization)

On the breach side, we’ve seen incidents involving payment processors, financial platforms, and large customer databases across different regions.

The pattern is familiar: critical flaws in common software get weaponized quickly, and many organizations are still slow to patch or detect the follow-up activity (webshells, persistence, lateral movement).

If you’re running anything exposed to the internet, especially PHP, Node, Java, or common enterprise tools, it’s worth checking your patch status and looking for signs of webshells or unusual processes.

🔒 CYBERSECURITY, PRIVACY & OPEN SOURCE ROUNDUP — November 24, 2026

1️⃣ GOOGLE PULLS AN EMERGENCY PATCH FOR A CRITICAL CHROME FLAW

Chrome 158.0.8127.88 and .89 are rolling out to Windows, macOS and Linux to close CVE-2026-134401, a critical bug serious enough that Google treated the release as emergency work rather than waiting for the regular cycle. Browser patches are the least glamorous and most consequential item on any patch calendar, because the browser is the one process that already holds your sessions, your cookies and your logged in identity, and a flaw reachable from a single page needs no cooperation from the victim. The update is incremental and silent, which is exactly why so many installs are still on the previous build weeks later.
🔹 @TheHackersNews

2️⃣ THE LINUX KERNEL JUST TOOK ON ONE HUNDRED AND SIX NEW CVEs

A single disclosure round assigned 106 new CVE identifiers to the kernel, the most aggressive batch in recent memory, with the worst rated 9.8: an out of bounds write in how NFSD handles SEQUENCE replies, tracked as CVE-2026-99362. The severity is not the surprise, the volume is. Modern kernels carry tens of millions of lines and a filesystem server compiled in by default on plenty of enterprise distributions, so a subsystem most administrators never think about is still reachable from the network. This is what scale costs in maintenance terms, and it is also why the kernel's stable release cadence is the actual security control here rather than any individual fix.
🔹 @cvedotnow

3️⃣ A SECOND VCENTER AUTH BYPASS LANDS DAYS AFTER THE FIRST WAS EXPLOITED

CVE-2026-123903, rated 9.8, lets anyone with network reach to vCenter skip authentication entirely, and it arrived only days after a nearly identical flaw was exploited in real attacks. Broadcom shipped patches covering twenty three vulnerabilities across ESXi, vCenter, Workstation and Fusion in the same window. Virtual infrastructure management sits at the top of the privilege ladder, one console that can walk every workload in a datacentre, which is why these bugs get attacked within hours of disclosure and why a management plane reachable from a general network segment is already a breach waiting on a scanner.
🔹 @TheHackersNews

4️⃣ A CLOUD SIDE FLAW PUT MALWARE ON HOME AND SMB ROUTERS

Attackers abused a weakness in a router vendor's cloud platform to install malware on customer routers and KVM devices with root level access, and the important operational detail is that the vendor fixed the cloud service, not the devices already sitting in racks. Anything with firmware that phones home to a managed portal inherits that portal's threat model, and a cloud patch does not rewrite flash memory on a device that was already rooted. Owners have to check their own hardware, because in this class of incident the vendor's definition of resolved and the customer's definition are not the same thing.
🔹 @TheHackersNews

5️⃣ VPN SOFTWARE IS BEING REBUILT TO MAKE TRAFFIC INVISIBLE

Researchers at Rapid7 linked a group called Webworm to a modified copy of an open source VPN client, altered so its traffic blends into normal encrypted connections, evades signature based detection and opens a covert path into internal networks. This is the quiet half of the encryption story, the same technology defenders recommend for privacy is repackaged by intruders as a tunnel that looks like everyone else's traffic. The uncomfortable consequence is that encrypted traffic inspection is already close to meaningless, so the real control sits in behavioural baselining and in what a device is allowed to reach after it authenticates.
🔹 @TheHackersNews

6️⃣ A FREE MAP OF WHO IS ACTUALLY EXPOSED WHEN A CVE DROPS

Project Discovery shipped SecurityContext 2.0, which cross references vulnerability data across open source: roughly 174 thousand repositories, 341 thousand packages, 66 native libraries and 411 thousand CVEs, queryable by repository, lockfile or SBOM. The value is not the CVE count, it is the answer to the question that eats an afternoon every time an advisory lands, whether the thing you actually ship is anywhere in that advisory's blast radius. Most teams already have the dependency files, they just have no way to ask them a question, and a tool that answers in seconds changes triage from guesswork into a lookup.
🔹 @pdiscoveryio

7️⃣ KAOS 2026.11 CUTS THE DESKTOP LOOSE FROM ITS OWN HISTORY

The latest KaOS release moved to a Niri and Noctalia 5 setup with dinit as init and greetd for the login screen, and removed Plasma and Qt5 completely rather than keeping them as a fallback, alongside Linux 7.2.15, Qt 6.12 and Mesa 26.3.1. Deleting a whole desktop environment is the part of open source maintenance nobody celebrates, it is unglamorous subtraction that keeps a distribution from carrying two decades of compatibility debt forever. A distribution that prunes is a distribution that still has an owner reading the dependency tree, and that is rarer than any new feature announcement.
🔹 @TheLinuxITGuy

8️⃣ ONE FLIPPED BIT WAS ENOUGH TO WALK PAST WINDOWS CODE INTEGRITY

A researcher from Google Project Zero showed that changing a single bit inside a .NET file was sufficient to get untrusted code running past Windows integrity checks, a flaw Microsoft closed back in October. Code integrity is supposed to be the layer that does not care what you type, the assumption that a binary either is or is not signed and unmodified. Finding the seam where that assumption leaks is how the whole chain of trust gets bypassed without ever touching an exploit, and it is a reminder that the strongest looking control is only as strong as the parser reading its metadata.
🔹 @TheHackersNews

💭 The pattern across all eight is that the decisive failure is rarely the bug itself. A browser patch nobody installed, a kernel with more surface than any team can audit, a management console reachable from the wrong network, a cloud fix that never touched the device, an open source client rebuilt by someone else, a dependency list nobody can query, a distribution brave enough to delete code, and an integrity check undone by one bit. Attackers keep winning on maintenance cadence and reachability rather than on sophistication, and every one of those is an operational decision, not a research breakthrough.

Which of these is sitting in your environment right now, a browser on an old build, a management console on a flat network, a dependency you have never actually queried? 👇

По данным Depthfirst, уязвимость phpAfterShell открывает путь атаки PHP2Shell: если операция перезаписи сессии будет прервана, злоумышленник, контролирующий актуальные данные, может инициировать десериализацию данных и RCE.

Уязвимость, получившая название phpAfterShell, отслеживается как CVE-2026-126714 (CVSS 9,2) и была устранена 19 ноября вместе с шестью другими критическими проблемами .

Исследователи Depthfirst отмечают: эта ошибка может позволить злоумышленнику, имеющему доступ к данным, записываемым в файл сессии, и способному прервать операцию записи сессии, инициировать десериализацию объекта и добиться RCE.

Это происходит потому, что PHP перезаписывает файл сессии с самого начала, не очищая его предварительно. Если операция прерывается в процессе записи или до того, как последующая операция усечения удалит старые данные, файл остается со смешанным содержимым: свежие данные сессии, за которыми следуют остатки старой сессии. 

Depthfirst нашла надежные методы прерывания файловой операции во время обновления хода загрузки сессии, что позволило им соединять префикс одной действительной сессии с суффиксом другой.

Последующая операция с сессией рассматривает поврежденные данные как легитимное состояние на стороне сервера, предоставляя злоумышленникам контроль над значениями сессии и возможность запускать десериализацию объектов.

Злоумышленник мог бы расположить новые и старые данные таким образом, чтобы объединенный файл интерпретировался иначе, чем исходные сессии, а части обычных строк превращались в сериализованные объектные данные. В будущей сессии эти объекты создавались бы и запускалась их десериализация.

В рекомендациях PHP отмечается, что прогресс загрузки сессии предоставляет удаленному клиенту один из способов повлиять на сохраненные данные сессии посредством многокомпонентной загрузки.

Та же основная проблема может возникнуть, когда приложение хранит в сессии большие строки, контролируемые пользователем. В многопоточных сборках PHP сбой, связанный с ограничением памяти в другом потоке, может завершить процесс во время записи в сессию.

Как объясняет Depthfirst, phpAfterShell связан с PHP2Shell, который возник из-за того, что во время анализа неаутентифицированного многокомпонентного запроса функция обратного вызова PHP для отслеживания прогресса загрузки могла открыть и декодировать сессию, связанную с файлом, до того, как начнется выполнение целевого скрипта.

Поскольку объекты становились активными во время вызова функции обратного вызова, PHP добавила ограничения на то, какие объекты могут быть созданы в памяти, но не изменил базовое поведение обновления файлов.

Даже с учетом новых ограничений функция обратного вызова по-прежнему считывает существующую сессию, добавляет состояние хода загрузки, сериализует все это и записывает обратно в тот же файл.

Для успешной эксплуатации уязвимости phpAfterShell необходимы определенные условия: активная работа хранилища сессий по умолчанию, путь эксплуатации (самый простой - отслеживание прогресса загрузки), остановка процесса PHP в процессе записи, запрос на вызов функции session_start() для поврежденного файла и путь от десериализации к выполнению кода.

Патчи для этой уязвимости были включены в версии PHP 8.6.0, 8.5.13, 8.4.28, 8.3.37 и 8.2.36. Сообщений об использовании phpAfterShell в реальных условиях, по всей видимости, нет. Но будем следить.

Zero-click bugs in messaging apps are treated as rare, bespoke findings, because reaching code that runs before a user taps anything means auditing a narrow slice of a huge application. That assumption shapes how vendors prioritize the work.

The speakers argue the assumption no longer holds. With the right tooling, LLMs can enumerate remotely reachable attack surface across messaging apps then audit it automatically.

Three case studies carry the argument: WeWorm, a WhatsApp zero-click affecting Samsung devices only, along with a nearly universal iOS one-click.

In their [un]prompted 2026 talk, "0-Click Remote Exploits in an AI World," on Tuesday, October 27 at 4:45 p.m. on Stage 1, Bruce Dang and Anna Groza present the tooling along with what changes once this research is cheap to automate.

Bruce Dang, Calif (presenter) Anna Groza, Security Researcher, Calif (presenter)

The session closes on trust boundaries: where the assumptions behind messaging app security break down, along with what platform vendors can do to shrink remotely exposed attack surface first.

Calif's OEMpocalypse research supplies the next stage, taking an unprivileged Android app to root across Samsung, Xiaomi, Oppo and OnePlus flagships.

GnuPG GPGME double free from a crafted OpenPGP key, CVE-2026-129975, 21 November 2026

Patch now: one bad key. 21 Nov 2026: GPGME has a critical double-free flaw. GPGME is the standard library that programs use to work with GnuPG. The CVE is CVE-2026-129975. GnuPG's internal id is T8557.

The official GnuPG advisory, sent on 20 November 2026, says an OpenPGP key with a crafted, very long user ID can trigger a double free. GnuPG says this double free can be used to exfiltrate data from applications, for example by sending signed data. GnuPG also says that exploiting the bug for remote code execution cannot be ruled out, and that an immediate update is highly suggested.

How it works

The root cause is in two GPGME internal functions that read status lines and key listings from gpg: read_status and read_colon_line. The advisory says a buffer of 1024 bytes is allocated first and is reallocated if more space is required. The new pointer is used inside the function, but is assigned back to the context object only at the end. If the function returns early, the context keeps a stale pointer to already-freed memory, which is then freed a second time. Tracker T8557 describes the same pattern in src/engine-gpg.c.

What is affected

The advisory says all software using a GPGME version prior to 2.3.0 is affected, as a shared library, a DLL, or statically linked. Version 2.3.0 was never publicly available.

GnuPG names these examples: Gpg4win, GnuPG Desktop, GnuPG VS-Desktop, most mail clients, many XMPP clients, Samba, and Flatpak. The advisory spells the last name as "Flatpack." It says new Gpg4win, GnuPG Desktop, and GnuPG VS-Desktop versions were released, but gives a version number only for Gpg4win: 5.1.2.

How severe

GnuPG rates the flaw a critical security bug. A CVSS score is unknown. As of 21 November 2026, NVD has no record for this CVE, and the https://t.co/I3F3ZJSvrJ page is still reserved.

Exploit status

The Hacker News reports that the project has not reported any attacks. A public exploit is unknown. The sources reviewed here do not report one. There is no interim workaround other than updating, or applying the patch attached to the advisory.

Who found it

The advisory says Johan Carlsson discovered the flaw, and that GnuPG was informed by GitLab on 12 November 2026. Disclosure was first set for 25 November 2026, then moved to 20 November 2026 because GitLab had to update earlier due to the Ruby2Shell bug.

Fix

Update GPGME to 2.3.1, dated 19 November 2026 in the advisory. For a Windows DLL, GnuPG points to Gpg4win 5.1.2. The official GPGME 1.24.4 NEWS file, dated 20 November 2026, says the legacy branch also fixes this double free. That NEWS file and the 1.24.4 readme warn that this is a legacy branch, and that the project cannot guarantee it will see all security patches.

If a program is statically linked, rebuild it against GPGME 2.3.1. If GPGME cannot be updated, apply the advisory patch. There is no need to update GPGMEPP or GPGMEQT.

Debian has fixed packages, per the official Debian tracker: 1.18.0-3+deb12u1 for bookworm, 1.24.2-3+deb13u1 for trixie, and 2.3.1-1 for sid. The tracker still lists forky 2.2.0-2 as vulnerable.

Every finding on the vulnerability report comes back critical, so the question is which one to patch first when the queue is longer than the week.

First, pull the CISA KEV catalog, the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities list. If a CVE is on it, someone is exploiting it in the wild, and that outranks any severity score. MOVEit CVE-2023-34362 sat on that list.

Next, check the EPSS score from FIRST, the Exploit Prediction Scoring System. It gives a probability of exploitation in the next 30 days. A high probability on a medium CVSS is a different problem from a low probability on a 9.8.

Then, read the CVSS base score for what it is, a severity snapshot that knows nothing about whether anyone is using the flaw today.

Finally, plan around the Windows Patch Tuesday cadence, and note where it stops helping. Log4Shell CVE-2021-44228 keeps turning up inside bundled third party software, and Windows Server 2012 has been out of support long enough that no Tuesday patch arrives at all.

An AI found a bug in Bitcoin.

On November 20, Bitcoin Core disclosed CVE-2026-117348. An AI scan from Project Loupe at Spiral found it.

The trick is simple. Repeat one transaction ID 50,000 times in a single message, and the node stalls for over 12 seconds. It processes nothing meanwhile, not even new blocks.

The fix is one line: process each announcement once. It shipped in versions 30.5, 31.3 and 32.1.

Lesson: the AI that writes your code now audits Bitcoin's. It found the bug first.

🚨 JUST IN: CVE-2026-117348 let a single peer stall Bitcoin nodes for over a dozen seconds, fixed in 30.5, 31.3 and 32.1.

No coins at risk, but a reminder to check your version. https://t.co/XY9xTDZLMM

One peer could freeze a Bitcoin Core node for over a dozen seconds per message, and while it's frozen the node processes no blocks from anyone.

The bug sat in the code since v29.0, and an AI scan caught it.

The advisory, CVE-2026-117348, is rated medium severity. Since v29.0 a node re-ran the missing-parent check every time an orphan transaction was announced again, with no deduplication.

• An attacker sends one orphan transaction with thousands of missing parents
• Then repeats its wtxid in inv messages up to 50,000 times
• Each message stalls the node for over a dozen seconds, during which it processes nothing from other peers, blocks included
• Affected: 29.0 to 29.5, 30.0 to 30.4 and 31.0 to 31.2
• Fixed in 30.5, 31.3 and 32.1

An automated LLM scan in Elias Rohrer's Project Loupe at Spiral flagged it on July 8, Gregory Sanders validated it, and another researcher reported it independently.

The stall is temporary and can't steal funds or permanently damage a node, so this is an annoyance and not a disaster. Still, a node that can't process blocks isn't doing the job you run it for, and the flaw sat across three release lines until the scan flagged it.

Worth being aware of if you run your own node on one of those versions.

AutoGPT is a workflow automation platform for creating, deploying, and managing continuous artificial intelligence agents. From versions 0.6.15 through 0.10.0, the value of a host-scoped credential header was exposed to other hosts via HTTP redirects. SendAuthenticatedWebRequestBlock attaches a host-scoped credential's headers to a request, but once a redirect took that request to a different origin, only three fixed header names (Authorization, Proxy-Authorization, Cookie) were removed. A host-scoped credential's header names are free-form (the UI suggests X-API-Key), so a credential carried under any other name followed the redirect to the new origin. This issue is fixed in version 0.11.0.

The vendored zcbor decoder's zcbor any skip() in boot/zcbor/src/zcbor decode.c descends one C-stack frame per level of CBOR nesting. On a list or map it copies the decoder state (memcpy(&state copy, state, sizeof(zcbor state t))) and recurses once per member, with no depth cap: the skip path does not use zcbor's backup stack, and ZCBOR MAX ELEM COUNT is SIZE MAX, so nothing bounds how deep the recursion goes.

That function is reached on attacker-controlled bytes before any authentication. MCUboot's serial-recovery command parser decodes SMP/CBOR requests with zcbor map decode bulk() (boot/boot serial/src/zcbor bulk.c), which skips any map key it does not recognise by calling zcbor any skip() on the encoded value; the echo handler in boot/boot serial/src/boot serial.c calls it directly on the same footing. Both run during image upload, long before the uploaded image's signature is checked. The default receive buffer is MCUBOOT SERIAL MAX RECEIVE SIZE = 512 bytes and each nesting level costs a single byte to encode (0x81), so roughly 500 levels of nesting fit in one request — comfortably more than a bootloader's stack can absorb, since every frame carries a full zcbor state t copy plus locals.

The impact is availability only: the bootloader's stack overflows and the device faults or hangs during recovery. There is no controlled out-of-bounds write that escapes the DFU buffer, no disclosure, and no authentication bypass — the recursion grows the stack with the decoder's own internal state. Whether a given board actually exhausts its stack depends on that board's bootloader stack size, which we did not measure; the fix is nevertheless unconditional, because an unauthenticated pre-authentication code path must not have its safety depend on a per-board stack margin.

Exposure requires MCUBOOT SERIAL (serial/SMP recovery), which is not enabled by default, and recovery entry is normally gated on a physical pin (CONFIG BOOT SERIAL ENTRANCE GPIO / PIN RESET), with a no-valid-image fallback path. Products that expose serial recovery over an externally reachable transport, or that fall into recovery when no valid image is present, are the ones at risk.

The fix is to bound the skip: thread a recursion-depth counter through zcbor any skip() (or have zcbor map decode bulk() reject values nested beyond a small constant) and fail once the limit is exceeded — equivalently, take the bounded-skip implementation from upstream zcbor.
